name: Sun exposure for acne
lead: Sun exposure for acne is the practice of tanning or sitting in sunlight to make blemishes look drier, less red and less noticeable. A tan evens out skin tone, so spots can appear to recede, and community members sometimes report a short-term improvement in how their skin looks.[3][4]

General acne references state that sunlight exposure is not associated with acne overall, that intense UVA can trigger a separate eruption called acne aestivalis, and that sun exposure can prolong postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, for which daily sunscreen is advised.[1] A clinic study of 400 women in Iran found that longer self-reported sun exposure was an independent predictor of post-acne pigmentation.[2]
People who discuss the topic on forums are divided: some say sun seems to help back and body acne, while others say a tan only masks spots and may worsen them over time.[3][4]
infobox: Drying and temporary clearing of blemishes

paras: Proponents say sun makes spots look drier and less inflamed for a time. A poster in a T Nation thread on back acne wrote that sun exposure seems to help, alongside washing and benzoyl peroxide.[3] Another poster in a T Nation acne thread argued that sun burns the epidermis and the evened-out skin only gives the impression that acne has receded.[4]
Wikipedia reports that sunlight is not generally associated with acne.[1]

Wikipedia notes that sun exposure can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and that daily SPF 15 or higher sunscreen can reduce that risk.[1] Acne aestivalis, a UVA-triggered polymorphous light eruption, typically appears on the arms, shoulders, back and chest and spares the face.[1]

Wikipedia's article on postinflammatory hyperpigmentation says UV exposure and sunburn contribute to the development, darkening and spread of pigmented lesions, that it is more common and more persistent in darker skin, and that it usually fades within 6 to 12 months untreated.[5]

No studies found specifically testing tanning as an acne treatment. A 2008 comparative study in Ardabil, Iran, of 400 women (200 with melasma and acne, 200 with acne alone) found post-acne pigmentation in 45.5% overall, 66.8% with melasma against 24.1% without; longer average sun exposure and higher melanin score independently predicted higher odds of post-acne pigmentation.[2][6]

lore.intro: Sun and acne come up in bodybuilding and skin-care forums, where users compare experiences with back and body acne.[3][4]

claims.claim: Sun exposure dries out and improves acne.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster reported that sun exposure seems to help back acne.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states sunlight is not generally associated with acne overall and that sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation.[1][5]

claims.claim: A tan only masks acne and may worsen it.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said a tan evens out the skin and gives a false impression that acne has receded.[4]
claims.experts: UV is documented to darken and spread post-inflammatory pigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis.[1][5]

card.summary: Tanning to dry out spots; reference sources link sun to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.
card.note: Sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation per general references.

quick.overview:
Some people tan or sunbathe in the hope of drying out acne. The effect, when reported, is described as temporary.

General references say sunlight is not associated with acne overall but can sustain post-acne dark marks.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say UV makes blemishes look drier and less red; no published trial supports it as a treatment.
quick.risks: UV can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis; sunscreen is advised by references.
